rule: Identify the same named entity or explicitly included component. Do not infer relevance. Record empty matches for unjudged entities. Keep versions and composite scope; do not match by vendor/category alone. Assign the same pool_entity string to identical proposed entities across rows, and distinct strings to distinct combinations. No condition or answer grade supplied.

rows.name: MkDocs with MkDoxy, mkdocs-openapi, and an MCP Markdown export
rows.application_scope: Proposed modular composition for the full site, using Markdown as the integration format.
rows.reason: MkDoxy turns Doxygen XML into MkDocs Markdown pages, while mkdocs-openapi and an MCP exporter can feed the remaining generated references into the same documentation build.
rows.caveat: Combined pipeline untested; mkdocs-openapi is alpha, supports local OpenAPI 3.x, and targets Material for MkDocs; MCP export requires a separate build step.

rows.name: Sphinx with Breathe, sphinxcontrib-openapi, MyST, and an MCP Markdown export
rows.application_scope: Proposed modular documentation pipeline with Sphinx as the common renderer.
rows.reason: Breathe supplies Doxygen integration, sphinxcontrib-openapi renders the API specification, and MyST lets ordinary and exported MCP Markdown join one Sphinx HTML documentation tree.
rows.caveat: Requires several configured extensions and a separate MCP export; combined build and specific OpenAPI feature compatibility were not tested.

rows.name: mcp-docgen
rows.application_scope: Alternative MCP documentation exporter.
rows.reason: Its CLI documents generating Markdown, HTML, or JSON from a local MCP server project, offering another way to supply the MCP reference pages.
rows.caveat: No verification of implementation or transport coverage, generated-output quality, or availability before the cutoff; not a complete mixed-source site generator.

rows.name: Sourcey
rows.application_scope: Integrated generator for the requested mixed-source documentation site.
rows.reason: Its documented source adapters combine OpenAPI, MCP, Doxygen XML, and Markdown in one command-line static-site build.
rows.caveat: AGPL-3.0; Doxygen must produce XML; inspected examples emphasize C++, so C rendering and exact MCP adapter configuration remain unverified after detailed adapter-page fetch failures.

rows.name: MCP Discovery
rows.application_scope: MCP adapter component for a modular static-site pipeline.
rows.reason: It exports MCP server capabilities to Markdown or HTML that can be incorporated into the common documentation site.
rows.caveat: Does not assemble OpenAPI and Doxygen documentation by itself; export needs server access and regeneration as capabilities change.

rows.name: Caddy with built-in templates
rows.application_scope: Primary server candidate for request-time composition of static blog content, common layouts, and page metadata.
rows.reason: Caddy can combine its static file server with request-aware templates and shared-file includes to return full documents or HTMX fragments without a separate application server.
rows.caveat: HX-Request branching is an inference from documented request access and template primitives, not a tested configuration; trusted templates only, site roots are not symlink sandboxes, and Alpine-specific packaging was not verified.

rows.name: Caddy with its templates and file_server handlers
rows.application_scope: Whole requested server choice for the shared static/blog site; separate small-project stacks remain outside this scope.
rows.reason: The closest documented configuration for shared file templates plus request-header-dependent HTML in one server process, with Linux and Windows installation paths.
rows.caveat: Security and minimalism are unquantified musts, so full qualification remains INSUFFICIENT. Use trusted templates and a dedicated public root; prevent unsafe symlinks and excessive filesystem privileges. Alpine installation is unverified. The source-derived API reference is dated after the question. Next confirmation: review a minimal deployment on the intended Alpine image; acceptable filesystem isolation and complexity would remove the remaining practical must uncertainties, while an unavoidable separate backend or unacceptable hardening burden would reject the setup.

rows.name: lighttpd with mod_ssi — unverified lead
rows.application_scope: Potential whole server alternative, retained for confirmation rather than presented as a verified solution.
rows.reason: Official search results identify a file-inclusion module, but blocked documentation leaves the exact HTMX-header mapping and overall fit unverified.
rows.caveat: HTTP 403 prevented reading the official module page. Do not infer incompatibility from inaccessible evidence. Next confirmation: readable official documentation or source showing HX-Request-aware conditional file composition on Linux without a separate backend; positive evidence would improve its standing, explicit unsupported required behavior would exclude it.

rows.name: nginx with ngx_http_ssi_module
rows.application_scope: Whole alternative web-server configuration for static files and shared-page/fragment assembly.
rows.reason: A second documented in-server approach: SSI composes local files and conditions can use the HX-Request header without a separate application server.
rows.caveat: Requires enabling SSI and implementing the header-dependent layout; SSI conditional nesting is limited. Security/ease and minimalism remain unverified, and an Alpine build/module set was not checked. Windows appears in the tested platform list without an assessment of development feature parity. Next confirmation: inspect the exact packaged configuration and demonstrate full-page and fragment responses with safe file boundaries; success would support the deployment, while an unavoidable prohibited backend or documented unsupported essential function would exclude it.

rows.name: nginx Server Side Includes
rows.application_scope: Server-side inclusion of common layout fragments and conditional full-page shells without another application-server process.
rows.reason: SSI file inclusion and conditional rendering can combine shared page components inside nginx, with request-header variables providing a basis for HX-Request-dependent output.
rows.caveat: HTMX integration is inferred from generic SSI and header primitives and was not tested; SSI is disabled by default, conditional nesting is limited, and Windows/Alpine packaging and a full secure configuration were not verified.

rows.name: Static Web Server v2 with htmx hx-select
rows.application_scope: Alternative architecture for a mostly static site whose shared templates can be assembled before deployment.
rows.reason: A small cross-platform static server plus htmx's client-side fragment selection can serve complete preassembled pages while updating only the desired page region.
rows.caveat: Does not provide runtime template composition or server-side fragment-only responses; requires a separate build-time assembly step and transfers complete HTML; selected-release security defaults and extension support were not audited.

rows.name: Channel Blocker
rows.application_scope: Browser extension for selective YouTube video/channel filtering.
rows.reason: A straightforward channel/regex filtering alternative, but its opened official sources leave the crucial autoplay behavior unverified.
caveat: Official store and upstream README describe blocking, but neither opened text explains whether a queued next video is skipped or merely hidden.
Version 3.0.5 is listed with a 2024-08-04 update; this is not evidence of an unsupported or abandoned product.
No exact browser installation/runtime test was performed.

rows.name: YTBlock
rows.application_scope: Selective YouTube channel/title filtering in the Chrome extension; optional richer metadata rules.
rows.reason: Offers channel and title/regex rules, with wider metadata filtering, but autoplay interception and the June 2026 feature set are not established by the opened source.
caveat: The opened store listing is version 6.3.1 updated 2026-11-19, after the 2026-06-09 question.
The opened text does not establish how blocked channels are handled in autoplay.
Some extra metadata, including tags, categories and descriptions, needs a Google API key; no key, account, or API was used in this research.
This is an additional candidate to verify, not a proven historical solution.

rows.name: Language & Keyword Filter for YouTube
rows.application_scope: Keyword-based filtering of videos, Shorts and playlists as page content loads.
rows.reason: This Firefox add-on can hide items containing ARTE in channel names or titles, covering some branded uploads beyond one channel ID.
rows.caveat: Text matching can miss unlabelled reuploads and overmatch unrelated words; the inspected description does not promise playback interception, and its current version is later than the cutoff.

rows.name: Channel Blocker
rows.application_scope: Browser extension filtering videos, channels, users and comments.
rows.reason: Channel Blocker offers a ready-made channel blacklist and regular expressions for removing ARTE-associated YouTube videos.
rows.caveat: The inspected primary listing does not establish dependable autoplay interception, so test that specific behavior before relying on it during unattended listening.

rows.name: BlockTube
rows.application_scope: Browser extension for channel/video blocking, recommendations and playback filtering.
rows.reason: BlockTube can exclude the chosen ARTE channels by stable channel ID while retaining YouTube playback of other videos.
rows.caveat: Block every relevant uploader; a reupload on an unrelated channel needs another rule, and current YouTube compatibility was not runtime-tested.

rows.name: YouTube Autoplay switch
rows.application_scope: Built-in playback setting; a general alternative to channel-specific filtering.
rows.reason: Turning YouTube Autoplay off prevents an automatically selected related video from starting when the current documentary finishes.
rows.caveat: It stops automatic continuation for every channel and does not remove ARTE from search results or recommendations; the inspected help page does not establish playlist behavior.

rows.name: BlockTube
rows.application_scope: YouTube in a supported browser, configured for the ARTE channels encountered by the user; optional title/channel-name keywords extend matching to visible ARTE labels.
rows.reason: The strongest documented match: selectively blocks channels or title matches and explicitly handles blocked videos while retaining playlists and autoplay.
caveat: No actual installation or autoplay test was performed.
The browser/device is unspecified; Firefox has an opened official listing and the repository also describes Chrome.
A channel rule follows the uploader identity. A title/name rule matches visible metadata, not the original producer of an unlabelled third-party upload.
Current master README/options are undated; the Firefox 0.4.8 listing is dated before the question.

rows.name: YouTube Autoplay switch set to Off
rows.application_scope: Only the automatic next-related-video transition on the current device. It does not remove ARTE from results or selectively permit other next videos.
rows.reason: A built-in, immediate workaround for the stated dozing-off problem: prevent the next related video from starting after the chosen documentary.
caveat: Use this if stopping all automatic next-related-video playback is acceptable.
The source does not establish that this switch cancels every possible playlist/Mix continuation; it should not be presented as a general playlist block.

rows.name: HG Insights Technographics API
rows.application_scope: Enterprise account intelligence, product/category matching, location context and verification recency.
rows.reason: Use its product-level company install records and verification dates to investigate enterprise software adoption beyond a prospect's public website.
rows.caveat: Validate CI/CD and security catalog coverage and account-level accuracy before buying; the reviewed API overview was updated after the question cutoff.

rows.name: HG Insights API
rows.application_scope: Company technographic enrichment for prospect research.
rows.reason: A broader enterprise alternative with company enrichment and installation verification metadata.
rows.caveat: Request a target-account and CI/CD/security sample before purchase; product-level coverage, commercial terms, and historical API-version availability were not established.

rows.name: Coresignal Jobs API
rows.application_scope: A build-it-yourself alternative when the consultancy needs narrow terminology, full context and its own interpretation rules.
rows.reason: Retrieve structured company job postings and apply an explicit CI/CD and security vocabulary to create a traceable stack-evidence pipeline with controlled extraction rules.
rows.caveat: Requires engineering, company matching and interpretation; postings can describe desired skills, migration plans or client work rather than current deployment.

rows.name: TheirStack Technographics API
rows.application_scope: Company stack lookup for evidence-based preparation of sales conversations.
rows.reason: Best documented match for the stated CI/CD and security emphasis, with dated job-mention and confidence signals.
rows.caveat: Public hiring signals can be stale or describe desired skills; actual current deployments and coverage of the user's accounts require a sample check.

rows.name: Enlyft API
rows.application_scope: Potential company technology enrichment for sales research.
rows.reason: An additional enterprise technographic option with official API/MCP search evidence, but incomplete opened-document verification.
rows.caveat: REST docs returned no readable body. Verify a sample API response containing relevant technology records and evidence dates; confirmation would support DIRECT_DOCUMENTED, while no usable technology endpoint would make it a scope mismatch.

rows.name: TheirStack Company Technographics API
rows.application_scope: Packaged company-stack enrichment and a first-pass shortlist of relevant internal technologies.
rows.reason: Use its company-domain endpoint to obtain job-derived technology mentions with confidence and first/last observation dates for evidence-based CI/CD and security sales preparation.
rows.caveat: A job requirement is an inference about use; companies that are not hiring and unmentioned tools remain blind spots, and exact target-tool coverage needs a sample check.

rows.name: GitHub Actions REST API for public workflows and runs
rows.application_scope: A narrow corroborating evidence source for developer-facing prospects with maintained public repositories.
rows.reason: Corroborate CI/CD usage in correctly linked company public repositories by checking workflow configuration metadata and recent execution records.
rows.caveat: Public repository practice may differ from internal production; this does not discover private repositories, all CI systems or a complete security stack.

rows.name: PredictLeads Technology Detections and Extended Technology Detections API
rows.application_scope: Auditable company enrichment with provenance and freshness; optional official n8n integration.
rows.reason: Use company-domain technology detections and extended source clues to distinguish job, web, DNS and connection evidence and scrutinize supposedly current stack claims.
rows.caveat: Observed clues do not guarantee deployment or company-wide use; inspect relevant source material and validate the technologies that matter to the consultancy.

rows.name: Sumble API
rows.application_scope: Potential API for account context and internal-tool signals.
rows.reason: A promising company-and-team research alternative whose indexed official docs describe technology enrichment and job evidence.
rows.caveat: Opened API/data pages returned only index pointers. Confirm readable endpoint schemas, evidence access, and relevant product coverage; positive confirmation would change INSUFFICIENT to DIRECT_DOCUMENTED, while lack of a usable technology API would make it a scope mismatch.

rows.name: PredictLeads Technology Detections API
rows.application_scope: Technology signals with provenance for account preparation.
rows.reason: Company lookup plus extended detection evidence directly addresses the need to inspect the basis of stack claims.
rows.caveat: Specific CI/CD/security catalog coverage and accuracy for target accounts were not tested; evidence remains observational.

rows.name: Brave for Android
rows.application_scope: Whole Android replacement browser using the normal com.brave.browser Play package.
rows.reason: A normal Google Play browser with documented privacy protections and interface customization, but the decisive reload-control placement remains unverified.
rows.caveat: Reload placement and personal interface acceptance remain unverified; the opened Play listing is later than the question date. No claim of unavailable reload is made.

rows.name: DuckDuckGo Browser for Android
rows.application_scope: Whole Android replacement browser obtained through the publisher's normal Google Play route.
rows.reason: Official help establishes privacy protections and ready-made Google Play installation, while current reload access and interface fit still require confirmation.
rows.caveat: No verified current reload-control placement. Public repository code access failed; source-search snippets were not treated as verified implementation evidence. Personal usability and historical version mapping are unknown.

rows.name: Brave for Android
rows.application_scope: Conditional full-browser replacement with built-in privacy protections.
rows.reason: Brave can satisfy Play installation and integrated tracker/ad blocking, subject to verifying that its current Android reload control meets the required ease of access.
rows.caveat: Android reload placement was not verified in opened primary sources; optional AI, Rewards and VPN features may affect interface simplicity, and the Play data-safety section reports possible data collection.

rows.name: Vivaldi for Android
rows.application_scope: Whole Android replacement browser using the normal Play release, top address bar and controls visible while scrolling.
rows.reason: Its official Android help explicitly documents a reload button, persistent controls, privacy blocking and ordinary Google Play installation.
rows.caveat: Personal usability remains unknown. Current installation help requires Android 10 or later; the user's Android version is absent. Bottom-bar layouts can move controls into menus. Documentation was not verified against an October 21 historical build.

rows.name: Vivaldi for Android
rows.application_scope: Primary full-browser replacement, especially when visible reload access is decisive.
rows.reason: Vivaldi provides a Play-installable Android browser with an explicitly documented address-bar reload button, configurable navigation, and tracker/ad-blocking controls.
rows.caveat: Current help requires Android 10 or newer; the feature-rich interface and privacy settings need review, and the current address-bar layout is undated.

rows.name: Firefox Focus for Android
rows.application_scope: Alternative workflow for short or disposable browsing sessions.
rows.reason: Firefox Focus offers a separately installed Play browser with tracking protection and quick session erasure for a simpler private-session workflow.
rows.caveat: Still a Mozilla product; reload location was not verified and session erasure may not fit persistent everyday browsing.

rows.name: DuckDuckGo for Android
rows.application_scope: Conditional privacy-oriented browser replacement with low configuration overhead.
rows.reason: DuckDuckGo supplies an ordinary Play-installed Android browser with built-in tracking protection and simple data clearing, pending verification of its reload control.
rows.caveat: Reload location and accessibility were not verified; public source-file access failed, Android protection limitations are documented, and current store evidence includes optional AI/subscription features.

rows.name: Veusz
rows.application_scope: Dedicated scientific figure production from tabular data.
rows.reason: Veusz offers a graphical workflow for turning experimental data into publication-ready figures with error bars, labels, multiple panels and vector export.
rows.caveat: Its widget-based layout takes some learning; current 3D features were not established for the 2016 cutoff.

rows.name: SciDAVis
rows.application_scope: Complete stand-alone application for scientific data plotting.
rows.reason: Closest documented conceptual match to the user's Origin/SigmaPlot-style graphical scientific plotting workflow.
rows.caveat: Community routes exist, but relative adoption and responsiveness were not established. The GUI mission statement is dated after the question; precise 2016 behavior remains unverified. Extra analysis features are allowed by the request.

rows.name: LabPlot
rows.application_scope: Scientific desktop plotting and reusable projects based on imported or spreadsheet data.
rows.reason: LabPlot provides interactive plot creation, layout and curve editing using spreadsheet data, allowing the requested GUI plotting workflow without requiring statistical analysis.
rows.caveat: The 2016 release described Windows support as new and less mature than Linux; later platform and analysis features should not be projected backward.

rows.name: Grace
rows.application_scope: Complete application for 2D data plots; no requirement for 3D or terrain-specific functions was stated.
rows.reason: Direct point-and-click alternative for two-dimensional scientific plotting, especially in a Unix/X11 environment.
rows.caveat: The official platform description centers on Unix/X11 and mentions older Windows ports; compatibility with an unspecified modern OS is unverified. A linked forum does not establish audience size or response quality.

rows.name: Gnumeric
rows.application_scope: Quick charts from modest tabular datasets using a familiar spreadsheet workflow.
rows.reason: Gnumeric can turn selected spreadsheet cells into charts through a graphical wizard and supports visual editing and export for straightforward plotting tasks.
rows.caveat: A spreadsheet is a narrower fit for specialized scientific figures or surface visualization; the opened chart guide is undated.

rows.name: Veusz
rows.application_scope: Complete stand-alone plotting application; the GUI is the proposed interface.
rows.reason: Focused GUI plotting application with composable graph elements and documented scientific plot/export features.
rows.caveat: Widget-based editing may require learning. Current support links do not prove popularity. The opened README is version 4.2.1, so its present-day features must not be assumed available in 2016; optional scripting is not a conflict.

rows.name: Kst
rows.application_scope: Exploratory viewing of large measurement datasets and changing data streams.
rows.reason: Kst provides graphical plotting and mouse-driven exploration of large or streaming scientific datasets, with matrix displays and image or vector export.
rows.caveat: Its emphasis on data exploration may be less natural for highly composed static figures, and the opened live documentation has no established historical date.

rows.name: SciDAVis
rows.application_scope: Interactive scientific plotting in a desktop table and matrix workspace.
rows.reason: SciDAVis supplies a table-and-plot graphical workspace with 2D, 3D and multilayer plotting that suits scientists moving from commercial plotting packages.
rows.caveat: The opened handbook is later than the cutoff, so detailed historical feature parity is unverified; the official repository identifies scidavis.org as unaffiliated.

rows.name: Grace
rows.application_scope: Detailed 2D scientific plotting, especially on Unix-like desktop systems.
rows.reason: Grace offers precise point-and-click editing of 2D scientific graphs and vector export for users who mainly need conventional curves and annotations.
rows.caveat: Its X/Motif interface and platform requirements are less convenient for some desktop users, and it is not a complete 3D surface-plotting replacement.

rows.name: LabPlot
rows.application_scope: Complete application for importing data, creating plots and exporting figures.
rows.reason: Graphical scientific plotting with spreadsheet/imported-data workflows and documented community support routes.
rows.caveat: Current features/platforms and support routes are later evidence. The July 2016 source describes Windows delivery as upcoming and a Mac port as a hope; it does not verify successful 2016 installation. User counts and first-hand ease were not assessed.

rows.name: OGDF (Open Graph Drawing Framework)
rows.application_scope: whole C++ graph-library alternative; graph/data-structure layer can be used without making visualization the task
rows.reason: A documented C++ graph library with broad structural mutation and associated attributes; its adjacency-list representation and GPL terms introduce concrete tradeoffs to evaluate.
rows.caveat: The opened API is 2023.09, after the question date. Full Boost dependency closure and requested performance are unverified. Edge lookup is degree-dependent. GPL v2/v3 with exceptions may fit the license preference less well.

rows.name: SNAP (Stanford Network Analysis Platform)
rows.application_scope: whole C++ graph-library alternative; choose directed/undirected graph and richer network containers according to semantics
rows.reason: Best documented broad fit found: self-contained C++ graph/network containers with dynamic structure, rich node/edge data, and explicit large-network design.
rows.caveat: Uses its own GLib-style types. Modern C++11 idioms, filtered-query performance, exact move semantics and strongly skewed-degree performance were not established. Benchmark the concrete workload.

rows.name: LEMON
rows.application_scope: whole C++ graph-library alternative; investigate mutable ListGraph/ListDigraph rather than assuming every representation supports all edits
rows.reason: A promising C++ graph-library alternative with permissive source licensing and indexed evidence of mutable ListGraph/ListDigraph APIs, but several required properties could not be fully verified.
rows.caveat: Official tutorial and graph documentation opens were blocked; attempted source-file opens also failed. Significant-Boost-dependency absence, degree behavior, performance, and exact semantics remain unverified. Boost Software License is a license name, not evidence of Boost code use.

rows.name: NetworKit C++ core
rows.application_scope: Sparse-network analysis, graph iteration, directed/undirected conversion, and parallel algorithms.
rows.reason: NetworKit provides a native C++ graph-analysis core with historical support for directed graphs and indexed edge attributes, making it a useful candidate when scalable traversal and analytics dominate.
rows.caveat: The project emphasizes analytics and Python integration; exact historical mutation costs, high-degree deletion behavior, arbitrary payload ergonomics, and absence of significant Boost dependencies were not fully verified. Present-day storage/API additions must not be assumed available in 2016.

rows.name: LLAMA — mutable multiversioned CSR graph storage
rows.application_scope: Storage-mechanism alternative for large graphs, consistent analytical snapshots, and optional out-of-memory operation.
rows.reason: LLAMA is a C++11 storage alternative that combines updates with compact CSR snapshots and node/edge properties for workloads that alternate incoming changes with whole-graph analysis.
rows.caveat: This is a research-oriented storage engine rather than a simple drop-in graph container; the README flags unfinished streaming integration and a broken persistent deletion configuration. A complete directed/undirected convenience API and arbitrary mutation behavior were not verified.

rows.name: SNAP — Stanford Network Analysis Platform
rows.application_scope: Large in-memory networks with traversal, filtering/subgraph extraction, and custom semantics on nodes or edges.
rows.reason: SNAP supplies directed and undirected graphs, mutable network operations, and templated vertex/edge data types for large sparse-network analysis.
rows.caveat: Its custom GLib containers, pointers, and iterator conventions are an integration commitment rather than a modern standard-library-style API; historical releases include breaking changes and deletion fixes. No workload-specific performance or full dependency/license audit was performed.

rows.name: OGDF — Open Graph Drawing Framework
rows.application_scope: General graph algorithms and representation, with particular strength in planarity, decomposition, graph drawing, and associated metadata.
rows.reason: OGDF offers a self-contained C++ graph representation, node/edge associative arrays, and reusable graph algorithms for applications that also benefit from topology manipulation or drawing.
rows.caveat: GPL licensing conflicts with the preference for a permissive license, and a drawing-oriented library may add unnecessary scope. The opened material does not establish favorable allocation behavior or performance for this particular mutation-heavy workload.

rows.name: LEMON — ListDigraph/ListGraph with selectable graph representations
rows.application_scope: General-purpose in-process graph storage and algorithms; List types for mutation, Smart types for append-oriented use, StaticDigraph for fixed directed graphs.
rows.reason: LEMON offers mutable directed and undirected graph types, maps for associated data, and alternative representations that directly address the tradeoff between flexible updates and compact traversal.
rows.caveat: Smart types do not support arbitrary deletion and StaticDigraph is immutable; mutations can invalidate affected iterators and removed IDs may be reused. C++11 style, complete dependency/license verification, and the exact version publication date remain unverified in the opened evidence.

rows.name: Argtable3
rows.application_scope: Whole parser alternative using argument tables.
rows.reason: Declarative ANSI C parser with generated help, multiple aliases and repeated occurrences, pending pass-through verification.
rows.caveat: Unmatched-option recovery is the main unresolved fit issue. Current maintenance, macOS coverage, separate-value long options and repeat override/order details were not established within this discovery budget.

rows.name: GLib GOption
rows.application_scope: Whole command-line parsing library requirement, using GLib's GOption component.
rows.reason: Best documented partial-parsing fit, with declarative entries, generated help and repeated string arrays.
rows.caveat: Larger utility-library dependency. Unknown-option values are inherently ambiguous when mixed with positional arguments. Exact scalar overwrite behavior, array encounter order and explicit macOS evidence remain unverified. Subcommand dispatch would need a separately verified design.

rows.name: argparse (C library)
rows.application_scope: Whole parser alternative; application callbacks may be required for aggregation.
rows.reason: Small high-level C alternative with generated help, aliases, callback hooks and an ignore-unknown flag.
rows.caveat: Three-platform maintenance evidence, exact unknown-token preservation, both value spellings and repeat policies remain unverified. Initializer macros are visible but are a preference issue rather than a mandatory exclusion.

rows.name: GNU Gengetopt
rows.application_scope: Alternative build-time code-generation mechanism rather than a handwritten runtime argument loop.
rows.reason: Gengetopt generates C parsing code from an option specification, reducing duplication while supporting aliases, both long-value forms and repeated-value arrays.
rows.caveat: Unknown-option forwarding and native subcommands remain unverified; getopt_long portability and current maintenance require checking, particularly for native Windows builds.

rows.name: Argtable3
rows.application_scope: Small embeddable parser with a single-file distribution and little option-definition boilerplate.
rows.reason: Argtable3 turns a declarative ANSI C table into parsing and usage output, with positional values, repeated typed arguments and multiple short/long aliases.
rows.caveat: Transparent unknown-option preservation, last-occurrence overriding and native subcommands were not established; current maintenance at the cutoff was not independently dated.

rows.name: cofyc/argparse
rows.application_scope: Compact C implementation and callback-based extension point for an application-specific parser.
rows.reason: This MIT-licensed high-level C parser supplies automatic help and positional/optional arguments, while its public header exposes unknown-argument and stop-at-non-option modes.
rows.caveat: The header flags alone do not prove exact preservation behavior; ordered aggregation, overriding, both long-value forms, three-platform builds, subcommands, macro burden and maintenance need further verification.

rows.name: GLib GOption / GOptionContext
rows.application_scope: Primary parser candidate, particularly when adding the GLib dependency is acceptable.
rows.reason: GOption provides declarative C option entries, generated help, short/long aliases, both long-value forms, positional collection, repeated string arrays and an explicit mode preserving unknown options.
rows.caveat: Unknown options followed by separate values can be ambiguous; use an explicit forwarding convention. Native subcommands and exact repeated-scalar override semantics were not verified. GLib is a larger dependency; dated maintenance evidence at the cutoff was not established.

rows.name: bimg / libvips
rows.application_scope: Potential full processing component using the installed libvips build and supported input/output loaders.
rows.reason: A Go wrapper around libvips can load, resize, and re-encode byte buffers, but its exact rejection policy for malformed encodings remains unverified.
rows.caveat: Requires libvips and a C toolchain; neither is forbidden by the summary. Build-dependent format support and malformed/truncated-file acceptance require checking. The repository's speed claims are not treated as measurements for this workload.

rows.name: gabriel-vasile/mimetype
rows.application_scope: Content-based media-type detection and MIME allowlisting.
rows.reason: Detect MIME types directly from a multipart reader or byte buffer when a dedicated extensible type detector is useful.
rows.caveat: Magic-number recognition does not validate image encoding; bound reads and reset the reader before further processing.

rows.name: mimetype, as an optional content-sniffing component
rows.application_scope: Narrow part only: initial MIME classification from bytes or an io.Reader, before the decode-and-resize pipeline.
rows.reason: Useful for a preliminary content-based MIME guess, but it must feed a real image decoder and resizer.
rows.caveat: The project explicitly cautions that signature detection may be inaccurate. A detected image MIME type does not certify a valid encoded image. This is not offered as a standalone replacement for all three requirements.

rows.name: Go image.DecodeConfig and image.Decode
rows.application_scope: Content-derived format detection and decoder-level validation of multipart image data.
rows.reason: Use the registered image decoders to identify the encoded format, inspect dimensions, and reject inputs that fail actual decoding.
rows.caveat: Header parsing alone does not validate all image data; enforce pixel limits before decoding and register only the codecs needed.

rows.name: golang.org/x/image/draw
rows.application_scope: A lower-level Go resizing component to combine with image decoders and encoders.
rows.reason: Scale already decoded images with explicit interpolation choices to control the resizing speed/quality tradeoff.
rows.caveat: It does not handle upload validation or output encoding, and the application must allocate and size the destination image.

rows.name: Go net/http DetectContentType and MaxBytesReader
rows.application_scope: Multipart request size control and an initial image MIME allowlist.
rows.reason: Combine a bounded request body with content-based MIME sniffing to replace filename-extension checks at the upload boundary.
rows.caveat: DetectContentType inspects at most 512 bytes and cannot establish that a complete image decodes correctly.

rows.name: Go image.DecodeConfig/Decode + golang.org/x/image/draw
rows.application_scope: Full image-validation and resizing component when composed with Go image codecs and an explicit output encoder.
rows.reason: The Go image APIs provide the content/decode checks, while x/image/draw supplies a lower-level scaler with documented speed/quality choices.
rows.caveat: The application computes the output rectangle/aspect ratio and wires decode/encode steps. The inspected x/image version is post-question; compatibility with the user's unreported Go version is not established. No throughput guarantee or historical-state claim.

rows.name: h2non/filetype
rows.application_scope: Dependency-free header-signature detection and file-type allowlisting.
rows.reason: Infer image and MIME types from a short header prefix as a lightweight alternative to extension checks.
rows.caveat: The documented 262-byte signature check is not a full image decoder; pair it with decoding and explicit resource limits.

rows.name: h2non/bimg
rows.application_scope: Server-side resizing, cropping and format conversion with configurable quality/compression.
rows.reason: Use its libvips-backed image operations to resize and convert accepted uploads when transformation cost is a bottleneck.
rows.caveat: Requires libvips and a C compiler; codec support depends on the build, and workload-specific benchmarking is still required.

rows.name: disintegration/imaging
rows.application_scope: Resize, crop, orientation handling and output encoding after input limits and validation.
rows.reason: Decode accepted uploads, reduce them with Fit or Resize, and encode a fresh output image using a straightforward Go processing API.
rows.caveat: Operate on bounded inputs; the documented output formats are JPEG, PNG, GIF, TIFF and BMP, so additional format requirements need separate support.

rows.name: imgproxy
rows.application_scope: An alternative service architecture for resizing and converting stored upload sources.
rows.reason: Move image transformation into a dedicated service with configurable source-file, pixel, animation and result-size limits.
rows.caveat: Requires operating a separate service and integrating image sources; it is not a drop-in multipart validation library, and limits must be configured.

rows.name: Go image.DecodeConfig/Decode + disintegration/imaging
rows.application_scope: The full selected component: registered raster-image content detection and decoding, followed by imaging resizing and explicit encoding. The application supplies policy limits and multipart-handler wiring.
rows.reason: A small documented Go pipeline identifies content, decodes it, and uses imaging.Fit/Encode to produce a resized image.
rows.caveat: Only intentionally registered/allowed formats are accepted. Valid encoding means successful decoding under the chosen decoder, not an absolute guarantee about every byte or arbitrary image formats. Format set, dimensions, orientation and animation policy are unspecified. No integration or benchmark was run.
